nameStory: Tree-skirt moss gets its charming name from the way it drapes around the base of trees like a Victorian lady's flowing skirt. It's also called 'poodle moss' because when dry, its curled and twisted branches create a fuzzy, poodle-like texture that's unmistakable to the touch.
description: Tree-skirt moss is a distinctive woodland moss that forms loose, trailing mats around the base of trees and on rocks. Its branches grow in an irregular, somewhat feathery pattern that creates a soft, draped appearance. The moss forms patches that can spread several inches across, with individual shoots reaching 2-4 inches long. When moist, it has a fresh green color, but it often appears yellowish-green to brownish when dry.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms loose, irregular mats that drape and trail over surfaces rather than growing in tight cushions or flat sheets

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: When dry, feels distinctly curly and poodle-like to the touch - branches twist and curl in a characteristic fuzzy texture

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Tiny leaves are arranged spirally around branches and tend to curve and twist when dry, giving the whole moss a crimped appearance

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost always found growing on tree bark, especially at the base of trunks, or occasionally on shaded rocks in wooded areas

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Bright green when wet, but often appears dull yellowish-green to brownish when dry - color change is quite dramatic

idTips.label: Branching
idTips.description: Branches irregularly and loosely, creating an open, airy structure rather than dense, tight growth

habitat: Tree-skirt moss thrives in moist, shaded woodlands throughout New England, particularly in mixed deciduous and coniferous forests. Look for it growing on the bark of living trees, especially at the base of trunks where humidity stays higher, and occasionally on shaded rocks or fallen logs. It prefers areas with consistent moisture and protection from direct sunlight.

seasonality.spring: Becomes vibrant green as spring moisture returns, making it much more noticeable against tree bark. This is when the moss is most lush and easiest to spot.
seasonality.summer: Remains visible but may appear duller during dry spells, taking on more yellowish tones. Still maintains its characteristic poodle-like texture when touched.
seasonality.fall: Often becomes more prominent again with increased rainfall and humidity. The distinctive curly texture becomes more pronounced as it cycles between wet and dry.
seasonality.winter: Persists through winter under snow cover, though less visible. On warmer winter days, it may appear quite green and fresh-looking.

funFact: Tree-skirt moss can survive being completely dried out for months, then spring back to vibrant green life within minutes of getting wet - it's like nature's own sponge that can resurrect itself from what looks like certain death!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other bark-growing mosses, but the distinctive 'poodle' texture when dry is unique - if you can gently scrunch it between your fingers and it feels curly and springy rather than flat or brittle, you've found tree-skirt moss.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its scientific name suggesting it belongs to the genus Anomodon, this moss has been reclassified into Pseudanomodon, which literally means 'false Anomodon' - botanists discovered it wasn't as closely related to true Anomodon mosses as originally thought.
compareHints: As the only Pseudanomodon species in New England, tree-skirt moss is most similar to members of the true Anomodon genus, but it differs by having more irregular branching and a looser, more trailing growth form. Unlike the denser, more regularly branching Anomodon mosses, tree-skirt moss creates that distinctive draped, poodle-like texture that's unmistakable once you've felt it.
